source.title: The Independence Prior of SAEs Fragments Visual Concepts
source.authors: Tommaso Mencattini; Giorgos Nikolaou; Donato Crisostomi; Thomas Fel; Francesco Montagna; E. Rodolà; Francesco Locatello

record.tranche_reason: The study measures SAE-feature polysemanticity on synthetic data and evaluates how spatial regularization and sparsifier choice affect it. This is a different measurement and setting from testing whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs.
record.gate_note: The study does not test individual neuron responses such as InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55. Its direct polysemanticity results are for learned SAE features on synthetic data; its real DINOv2 results are proxies for feature interpretability, not neuron polysemanticity. The superposition-ratio sweep varies a benchmark setting but does not establish the proposed causal explanation for neuron polysemanticity. Results on MCC, F1, region coherence, and automated ratings are not separately recorded where they do not measure polysemanticity or its reconstruction tradeoff.
record.test_reason: The study measures the polysemanticity of learned SAE dictionary atoms, not neurons of any model. It compares its own method (Spatial-SAE) against baseline SAEs on synthetic data with known dictionaries, then uses interpretability proxies on DINOv2. It relies on the superposition/linear-representation framework as a premise and reports only its method's performance. It does not report how often model neurons, in vision or language models, respond to unrelated inputs. Reducing SAE-atom polysemanticity via a spatial prior is a related but different construct from V5, which concerns the share of polysemantic neurons in the network itself as activation function or architecture vary.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that tokenwise SAEs implicitly assume patch independence, which vision activations violate. Their Spatial-SAE reduces SAE-feature polysemanticity and improves concept recovery on synthetic data. On DINOv2 it improves every interpretability proxy, trading reconstruction concentrated at high spatial frequencies, framed as moving along the rate–distortion–polysemanticity frontier. They add that JumpReLU improves R2 as well, and that a mistuned trace coefficient can erase or reverse gains in the capacity sweep.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains spatially regularized sparse autoencoders and evaluates recovered SAE features; it does not use the original neuron-visualization procedure or the Softmax Linear Units method.
record.method_sensitivity: Polysemanticity results vary with sparsifier and trace strength; in the capacity sweep, high trace strength can worsen polysemanticity, particularly relative to the decomposed model.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding a spatial Markov-field prior to SAEs lowers the polysemanticity of the learned SAE atoms on synthetic spatial data. Strict win rates are 87.7–100% across four sparsifiers. This usually costs reconstruction R2, except for JumpReLU. Results depend on the trace strength: at high µ, polysemanticity worsens in 49% of capacity cells relative to the unregularized two-stream model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Polysemanticity of sparse-autoencoder dictionary features (not model neurons) depends on the SAE's inductive prior and can be reduced by spatial regularization, at some reconstruction cost.

record.code_released: The authors say they will publicly release code, datasets, and trained models upon publication; implementation extends https://github.com/KempnerInstitute/overcomplete
record.problems: The direct polysemanticity results are on synthetic SAE features, not individual neurons; the real-image experiments cannot measure polysemanticity against a ground-truth dictionary and instead use interpretability proxies. Table 1 reports aggregate win rates without effect sizes or uncertainty for those rates.
record.rows_left_out: MCC and support-F1 win rates in Table 1 and Table 2, and real-image normalized F1, region coherence, and automated ratings, are not separately recorded because they do not directly measure the polysemanticity outcome in V5.

untested.parts: No individual neurons of image classifiers are examined.
No language-model MLP neurons are examined.
The superposition ratio is varied only as a synthetic-data generator parameter for SAE recovery. There is no test of whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by superposition.

No measurement of the share of polysemantic neurons in a model under different activation functions, architectures or regularizers. Only SAE-atom polysemanticity under the authors' own spatial prior is measured.
Not addressed for neurons. The SAE polysemanticity metric is borrowed and is not varied.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' for V5 conflates SAE-atom polysemanticity with neuron polysemanticity. The SAE is an analysis tool, and all rows compare the authors' method against baselines. No verdicts are given. Neither original source is involved.

versions.untested_parts: Individual neurons in image classifiers and their responses to unrelated image inputs.
MLP neurons in transformer language models and their responses to tokens or contexts.

Whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by sparse features being packed together under capacity pressure. The synthetic sweep varies superposition and capacity but does not test this causal account of neuron responses.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when there is enough capacity for every feature.
The study tests spatial regularization and sparsifier differences for SAE features, not the share of polysemantic neurons; it does not test SoLU or modern convolutional networks.
Whether canonical mixed-responding neurons detect a shared feature or related subfeatures.
Whether neuron polysemanticity classifications change with activation-range selection or explanation-scoring choices.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Synthetic benchmark comparisons across the four tested sparsifiers
reader_labels.reason: S_PATIAL-SAE lowers the reported SAE-feature polysemanticity metric in 87.7%–100% of matched comparisons; for JumpReLU it also strictly improves R2 in all comparisons (r1–r4, r8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Reconstruction outcomes for TopK, BatchTopK, and ReLU; high trace strength in the capacity sweep
reader_labels.reason: The first three sparsifiers have no strict R2 wins, while a high trace strength worsens polysemanticity in some capacity settings and worsens it in 49% of configurations against D (r5–r7, r10–r11). The win-rate data do not establish the magnitude of the reconstruction cost.
